verses.text: The children of Israel did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight: and Yahweh delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years.
The hand of Midian prevailed against Israel; and because of Midian the children of Israel made themselves the dens which are in the mountains, and the caves, and the strongholds.
So it was, when Israel had sown, that the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up against them.
They encamped against them, and destroyed the increase of the earth, until you come to Gaza. They left no sustenance in Israel, and no sheep, ox, or donkey.
For they came up with their livestock and their tents. They came in as locusts for multitude. Both they and their camels were without number; and they came into the land to destroy it.
Israel was brought very low because of Midian; and the children of Israel cried to Yahweh.
When the children of Israel cried to Yahweh because of Midian,
Yahweh sent a prophet to the children of Israel; and he said to them, “Yahweh says, the God of Israel, ‘I brought you up from Egypt, and brought you out of the house of bondage.
I delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out from before you, and gave you their land.
I said to you, “I am Yahweh your God. You shall not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.” But you have not listened to my voice.’”
Yahweh’s angel came, and sat under the oak which was in Ophrah, that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. His son Gideon was beating out wheat in the wine press, to hide it from the Midianites.
Yahweh’s angel appeared to him, and said to him, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!”

Gideon said to him, “Oh, my lord, if Yahweh is with us, why then has all this happened to us? Where are all his wondrous works which our fathers told us of, saying, ‘Didn’t Yahweh bring us up from Egypt?’ But now Yahweh has cast us off, and delivered us into the hand of Midian.”
Yahweh looked at him, and said, “Go in this your might, and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Haven’t I sent you?”
He said to him, “O Lord,  how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”
Yahweh said to him, “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.”
He said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, then show me a sign that it is you who talk with me.
Please don’t go away, until I come to you, and bring out my present, and lay it before you.” He said, “I will wait until you come back.”

Gideon went in and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes of an ephah  of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.
The angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and lay them on this rock, and pour out the broth.” He did so.

Then Yahweh’s angel stretched out the end of the staff that was in his hand, and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes; and fire went up out of the rock, and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. Then Yahweh’s angel departed out of his sight.
Gideon saw that he was Yahweh’s angel; and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! Because I have seen Yahweh’s angel face to face!”
Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”
Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.”  To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
That same night, Yahweh said to him, “Take your father’s bull, even the second bull seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is by it.
Then build an altar to Yahweh your God on the top of this stronghold, in an orderly way, and take the second bull, and offer a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah which you shall cut down.”
Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as Yahweh had spoken to him. Because he feared his father’s household and the men of the city, he could not do it by day, but he did it by night.

When the men of the city arose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah was cut down that was by it, and the second bull was offered on the altar that was built.
They said to one another, “Who has done this thing?” When they inquired and asked, they said, “Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing.”
Then the men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son, that he may die, because he has broken down the altar of Baal, and because he has cut down the Asherah that was by it.”

Joash said to all who stood against him, “Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? He who will contend for him, let him be put to death by morning! If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because someone has broken down his altar!”
Therefore on that day he named him Jerub-Baal,  saying, “Let Baal contend against him, because he has broken down his altar.”
Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east assembled themselves together; and they passed over, and encamped in the valley of Jezreel.
But Yahweh’s Spirit came on Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together to follow him.
He sent messengers throughout all Manasseh; and they also were gathered together to follow him. He sent messengers to Asher, and to Zebulun, and to Naphtali; and they came up to meet them.
Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken,

behold, I will put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor; if there is dew on the fleece only, and it is dry on all the ground, then shall I know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.”
It was so; for he rose up early on the next day, and pressed the fleece together, and wrung the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.

Gideon said to God, “Don’t let your anger be kindled against me, and I will speak but this once. Please let me make a trial just this once with the fleece. Let it now be dry only on the fleece, and on all the ground let there be dew.”
God did so that night; for it was dry on the fleece only, and there was dew on all the ground.

footnotes.content: The Lord permitted Israel's evil to bring them into Midian's hand—not to destroy them, but to teach them. When we drift from His way, He doesn't leave us; He lets us feel the weight of our separation until we cry out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear drove Israel into caves and dens like hunted animals. When we run from truth instead of toward God, we hide ourselves away. The mountain strongholds could not save them—only returning to the Lord could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every harvest season, the Midianites and their allies swept down like a plague. The very thing Israel had worked for turned to dust. The Lord was showing them their need: you cannot prosper in rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They left nothing—no sheep, no oxen, no donkeys. Emptiness and hunger have a way of making us listen. The Lord was stripping away everything Israel trusted in except Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Locusts have no number—an image of helplessness against something vast and unstoppable. Israel could do nothing against such a tide. When we are at the end of ourselves, the Lord is often at the beginning of His work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Brought very low—this is where repentance begins. After years of hiding and losing everything, Israel finally cried out. The Lord heard them at their breaking point, just as He hears us when pride falls away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their cry reached heaven. This verse pauses us at the threshold—Israel has spoken, and now the Lord responds. Even our stammering, uncertain prayer finds His ear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A prophet came first, not a warrior. The Lord spoke to remind Israel before He raised them up. Words of covenant—Egypt, bondage, deliverance—awakened their memory of His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord recited His own faithfulness: Egypt, enemies driven out, land given. He was telling Israel, 'I am the same God who saved your fathers. Have you forgotten Me already?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear the Lord, not the gods of this land—Amorite gods were powerless shadows, yet Israel chased them. The prophet's charge cut straight to the heart: obedience begins with whom we truly fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Under the oak at Ophrah, hiding wheat in a wine press—Gideon worked in fear, yet the Lord found him there. He was nobody, but the Lord's angel came. Grace meets us not in the spotlight but in our small, anxious work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mighty man of valor—the Lord called Gideon by what he would become, not what he was. This is how the Lord speaks to His servants: not 'you are small' but 'I am with you, and you are mighty in Me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon's doubt poured out: 'Where are His wonders? We are cast off.' How honest is this prayer. He had not yet learned that the Lord's silence is never absence—it is often the prelude to His greatest works.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord did not argue with Gideon's despair; He redirected it. 'Go in this your might'—strength was already present, hidden beneath the fear. The Lord sees what we cannot yet see in ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My family is the poorest, I am the least—Gideon's humility was real, and his objection was reasonable by human reckoning. Yet the Lord has always chosen the weak to confound the strong and show His glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not 'You will be mighty' but 'You shall strike as one man with Me.' Gideon's victory was never his alone—it was the Lord's presence making one man the equal of multitudes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon asked for a sign, for assurance—and the Lord did not rebuke him for it. Faith is not always sudden; sometimes it grows through a humble asking, 'Lord, show me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon offered hospitality—a gift of meat and bread prepared with his own hands. The angel agreed to wait. Even our small, careful offerings are received with patient kindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon brought an ephah of meal, unleavened cakes, meat in a basket, broth in a pot. Every detail speaks of his care and his poverty. What he had, he gave. The Lord sees the heart behind the offering, not the size of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel commanded: lay the meat and cakes on the rock, pour out the broth. Gideon obeyed the specific instruction without hesitation. Obedience to the small word prepares us for the great work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fire from the rock consumed the offering—a sign unmistakable. The Lord's touch transforms what we offer into something wholly other. Then the angel vanished, and Gideon was alone with the knowledge of whom he had seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Face to face with the angel—Gideon's terror broke the silence. 'I will surely die' was the ancient cry when mortals glimpse the Holy. Yet the Lord had other plans for that frightened man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peace be to you. Don't be afraid. You shall not die. Three words that still echo: mercy spoken to the trembling. When we stand before the Lord in our smallness, His first word is always peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon built an altar and called it Yahweh-Shalom, the Lord is Peace. That stone stood in Ophrah as a witness—to Gideon's encounter, to God's keeping, to the quiet that settles on a soul who has met the Holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That very night, the Lord asked Gideon to strike at Baal's altar in his own father's house. Obedience would cost him—his family's anger, the city's rage. Yet the Lord's command came gently: 'Go in this your might.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Build an altar to the Lord on the stronghold, use the Asherah's wood for the burnt offering. The Lord was teaching Gideon: what Israel has bowed to must be broken, then transformed into an offering to the true God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon took ten servants and did it by night, afraid of his father's household and the city. His fear was not cowardice—it was wisdom about consequences. Yet he obeyed the Lord first, and accepted the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the morning, the city awoke to find Baal's altar broken and a burnt offering smoking on a new altar to the Lord. The work was done. No violence, no argument—just the silent work of faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who has done this? The city's shock gave way to investigation. Gideon's secret deed became known. There is a freedom that comes when we stop hiding—when our obedience to the Lord is openly seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bring out your son, that he may die—the city's rage turned on Joash, Gideon's father. In that moment, what would Joash do? Would he protect his son or bow to the mob's gods?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joash stood and defended his son: 'If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself.' A pagan father spoke a truth that shamed his people—if Baal is real, he needs no men's hands to save him. Gideon's obedience had vindicated itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerub-Baal—Let Baal Contend—became Gideon's new name. It was a name of mockery at first, then a name of power. The Lord had turned Gideon's act of breaking the idol into a standing witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Midianites and their allies gathered at Jezreel—sensing their opportunity slipping away, they gathered all their forces. The test was coming. Gideon had broken the idol; now he would face the sword.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon and he blew the trumpet. Not by his own courage, but by the Lord's empowering, he summoned Abiezer. The Holy Spirit still comes upon the obedient and makes them instruments of His will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon sent messengers to Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali—calling Israel's tribes to gather. One man who had hidden in fear was now calling warriors to battle. The Lord's Spirit had transformed the trembling servant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon spoke to God again: 'If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.' Even now, standing on the brink of battle, Gideon asked for reassurance. The Lord honored his honest heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor—Gideon's fleece became a sign. The Lord had not forbidden it; He permitted Gideon's search for confirmation. Sometimes faith needs time to settle into certainty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning came, and Gideon wrung out the fleece—a bowl full of water, while the ground was dry. The Lord answered with precision. He does not mock our seeking; He meets us where we are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon asked once more—reverse the sign, this time let the fleece be dry and the ground wet. He was bold enough to ask again, and humble enough to beg the Lord's pardon for his repeated doubt. This is the prayer of a struggling heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That night, the Lord did exactly as Gideon asked—the fleece stayed dry, the ground turned wet. Readers today hear an echo in this: the Lord's patience with our slow faith. He does not despise the seeker who asks again and again. We know now that He waited thousands of years to speak His final Word in Jesus, and still waits for each of us to answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
